evidence_items.publisher: BMJ Open; abstract indexed by PubMed
evidence_items.explanation: The April publication reports substantial problems across five chatbots, supporting caution about medical advice. Its adversarial prompts tested February 2025 systems; 49.6% of responses were problematic, including 19.6% highly problematic, rather than nearly half being highly problematic.

evidence_items.publisher: JAMA Network Open; abstract indexed by PubMed
evidence_items.locator: Abstract, Conclusions and relevance; bibliographic record
evidence_items.explanation: This April paper evaluated 21 models across 29 clinical scenarios and concluded that they remained insufficient for safe deployment. Stronger final-diagnosis performance accompanied weaker differential diagnosis; this was not a trial of patients using chatbots.

The randomized study involved 1,298 participants and found that model-assisted users performed no better than controls at identifying conditions and choosing care. Its much stronger model-only condition-identification results limit any inference that the models lacked medical knowledge altogether.

evidence_items.locator: Publication header naming Nature Medicine and February 23, 2026; Abstract
evidence_items.explanation: The header places this fourth paper in Nature Medicine, also the journal for e3: the four papers appeared in three journals. Its medical findings nevertheless support caution, including roughly 52% emergency undertriage in a structured stress test.

A later reanalysis found that measured triage errors varied with output format and scoring. It tested different API systems rather than ChatGPT Health, so it limits generalization but does not overturn the original product's findings or the earlier publication record.

unresolved_gaps: These studies do not establish a single error rate for ordinary medical chatbot use or every model available at the post date.
